passages.title: Email Correspondence: Notification of a Data Breach

emails.subject: Important: a security incident affecting your account
emails.body:
Dear Customer,

We are writing to tell you about a security incident. On 24 September we detected unauthorised access to one of our order-processing systems. We believe the access began on 18 September and ended when we closed it on 24 September.

The affected system held names, email addresses, delivery addresses and order histories. It did not hold payment card details, which are processed by a separate provider and are never stored on our systems. It did not hold passwords in readable form; passwords are stored using a one-way function and cannot be recovered from what was taken.

We have reported the incident to the privacy commissioner and engaged an external firm to review how the access occurred. We have also reset the session tokens for every account, which is why you may have been signed out.

You do not need to change your password, but you may wish to if you have used the same one on other sites. We will never contact you by telephone about this incident, and we will never ask you for a password or payment details. If you receive such a call, it is not from us.

We are sorry. We will write again when the external review concludes.

Meridian Books Security Team

emails.subject: Follow-up: findings of the external review
emails.body:
Dear Customer,

As promised, we are writing with the findings of the external review into the incident reported on 2 October.

The access was gained through a third-party plug-in used for address validation. A security update for that plug-in had been released in July. Our process required updates to be applied within thirty days, and this one was not applied. That is the direct cause, and it was our failure, not the supplier's.

The review confirmed our earlier statement in one respect and corrected it in another. Payment card details were not affected, as we said. However, the affected system also held customer telephone numbers, which our first notice did not mention because they sat in a linked table the initial assessment did not examine. We are telling you now rather than waiting for the final report, because you are entitled to know what was actually taken.

We have made three changes: updates to third-party components are now applied automatically rather than manually, an inventory of every component with access to customer data is reviewed monthly, and the initial assessment procedure now requires linked tables to be examined before any notice is issued.

We understand that a correction of this kind reduces confidence rather than restoring it. We would rather correct the record than leave it wrong.

Meridian Books Security Team

passages.title: Why Password Advice Changed
passages.content:
For twenty years the standard advice about passwords was consistent and, it turns out, largely wrong. Users were told to choose short, complex strings mixing cases, digits and symbols, and to change them every ninety days. Most large organisations enforced both rules. Both have now been withdrawn from the major guidelines, and the reasoning is worth understanding because the old habits persist.

The complexity rule failed because it assumed the attacker was a person guessing. Against software testing billions of combinations, a short complex password is weak; length is what defeats it. A sixteen-character phrase of ordinary words has vastly more possible combinations than an eight-character string of symbols, and is far easier to remember. The old rule also produced predictable behaviour: told to add a capital and a digit, people capitalised the first letter and appended a one.

Forced expiry failed for a related reason. When required to change a password every ninety days, users made the smallest change permitted — Summer2024 became Summer2025 — which an attacker who has one password can guess trivially. Expiry also encouraged writing passwords down in accessible places. Current guidance is to change a password when there is reason to believe it has been exposed, and not otherwise.

What replaced these rules is less about the password itself. The first recommendation is a unique password for every account, which is impossible to do from memory and is the reason password managers are now recommended by the same bodies that once discouraged them. The second is multi-factor authentication, which matters more than any property of the password: a stolen password alone is not enough to enter.

Not all second factors are equal. A code sent by text message is far better than nothing but can be intercepted by an attacker who persuades a mobile provider to transfer a number. An authenticator application avoids that, and a physical security key avoids more still. Most people do not need a physical key; almost everyone benefits from moving off text messages for their email account, which is usually the account that can reset all the others.

That last point is the one worth acting on. Email is the recovery route for most services, so its compromise cascades. Securing it well is worth more than improving every other password combined.

passages.title: Should Smartphones Be Banned in Secondary Schools?

viewpoints.name: Ravi Menon, secondary school principal
viewpoints.text: We locked phones away in pouches at the start of last year and the change in the corridors was immediate and obvious. Not the test scores — I make no claim there yet — but the noise, the eye contact, the number of students actually talking at lunch. What surprised me was how many students told us afterwards that they were relieved. Being reachable at all times is a burden they did not choose and could not put down while everyone else carried one.

viewpoints.name: Bethan Price, parent
viewpoints.text: I supported the ban until my daughter's bus was cancelled in a storm and she had no way to reach me for forty minutes. I am not arguing for phones in lessons; I am arguing that a total ban solves a classroom problem by creating a safety problem, and the people who design these policies rarely have a child travelling an hour each way. Collect them at the classroom door and give them back at the gate. That is not complicated.

viewpoints.name: Dr Farrah Nazir, education researcher
viewpoints.text: The honest summary is that the evidence is weaker than both sides claim. The studies most often quoted are small, and the largest ones show a benefit concentrated among lower-attaining students rather than across the board — which is interesting and worth acting on, but is not the same as a general effect. I would add that a ban is easy to announce and hard to enforce consistently, and a rule enforced unevenly teaches something worse than the rule was meant to fix.

viewpoints.name: Owen Baptiste, teacher
viewpoints.text: I am the person who has to enforce whatever is decided, and that is missing from most of this conversation. Before the ban I spent a measurable part of every lesson on phone confiscation arguments, and those arguments poisoned relationships with exactly the students I most needed on side. The pouch system moved that conflict to the school gate and out of my classroom. Whatever the research eventually says about attainment, that alone changed my working life.
